query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, prolonged exposure to intermediate/high service temperatures induces subtle grain-boundary segregation of specific elements (due to slight differences in diffusion rates) that nucleates nanoscale, incoherent brittle precipitates; these intergranular features compromise grain-boundary cohesion and lead to emergent brittle behavior, contrary to the rapid, large-scale precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, homogenous single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic or near-equiatomic alloy with a uniform solid solution and no pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates).
generation.intervention: Isothermal thermal aging at a temperature in the intermediate-to-high range (e.g., 700–900 °C) for prolonged durations to simulate service conditions.
generation.conditions: Aging performed in an inert atmosphere (or vacuum) to avoid oxidation, followed by standardized tensile and fracture toughness tests; microstructural analysis (TEM, EDS) conducted on specimens aged under controlled times versus unaged controls.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale intergranular precipitates formed from localized compositional segregation along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Due to differential, albeit sluggish, diffusion of the constituent elements in a HEA, certain species gradually segregate to the grain boundaries during thermal exposure. This localized enrichment surpasses the energetic threshold for precipitate nucleation, leading to the formation of brittle, incoherent intermetallic-like phases that degrade grain-boundary cohesion and reduce overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-processed, ductile baseline, aged HEA specimens are expected to exhibit reduced ductility and fracture toughness, with microstructural evidence (via TEM/EDS) of nanoscale precipitates decorating the grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The initial, unaged single-phase alloy which displays high toughness and a uniform distribution of elements without intergranular precipitates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to be active under service-like thermal conditions (700–900 °C) over extended time periods; it may not manifest at lower temperatures where atomic mobility is insufficient or under conditions that promote rapid, bulk precipitation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature–time thresholds for the onset of segregation and precipitate formation, as well as the influence of slight compositional variations, remain uncertain and may vary between different HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identically processed single-phase HEA specimens. Divide the batch into two groups: one group is aged isothermally at a service-relevant temperature (e.g., 800 °C) for an extended period (e.g., 1000 hours) in an inert atmosphere, simulating long-term service exposure, while the control group is retained in the as-processed condition. After aging, perform tensile and fracture toughness tests and examine grain-boundary microstructures using TEM combined with EDS.
measurements: Yield strength and elongation at fracture
TEM imaging and EDS compositional analysis of grain boundaries to detect the presence and morphology of nanoscale precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in toughness or ductility relative to the unaged controls, and if microstructural analyses fail to reveal the formation of nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates or segregation patterns, then the hypothesis that thermally induced grain-boundary segregation leads to brittle behavior in these HEAs is falsified.

System: Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) and 316 H stainless steel reference. Processing: Arc melting to produce 50g ingots, followed by high-temperature homogenization at 1200 °C for 48 hours in a vacuum environment with a titanium getter, then air-cooling; samples exposed to purified FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours. Question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) using in-situ alloy formation from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence microstructure, defects, and mechanical properties?. System: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 refractory metal high entropy alloy (50 at% V, 20 at% W, 20 at% Mo, 20 at% Ta, 20 at% Nb in initial mix with 1.5x V compensation). Processing: Laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm, 70 µm beam diameter) on Mo substrates; two parameter sets tested: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch); volumetric energy densities of 125 J/mm³ and 889 J/mm³ respectively; argon shielding gas with <25 ppm O2. Test conditions: Samples built as 6 × 6 × 6 mm³ cubes; analyzed via SEM, EBSD, TEM, EDS, and microhardness testing; relative density measured by optical microscopy; microhardness measured at HV0.1 load.
